title: Januvia and Alcohol: Pancreatitis Risk, Low Blood Sugar and Safety
excerpt: Can you drink on Januvia (sitagliptin)? How the drug works, why pancreatitis is the main alcohol concern, when low blood sugar is a real risk, and what changes if you take Janumet.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Januvia (sitagliptin)? Pancreatitis risk, when low blood sugar matters, the Janumet metformin warning, and signs that need a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Januvia (sitagliptin) doesn't have a direct chemical clash with alcohol. It isn't broken down by the liver in a way alcohol interferes with, and on its own it rarely causes low blood sugar. That's why many people who take it can have an occasional drink if their doctor agrees. The real concerns are indirect. Heavy drinking is one of the most common causes of **pancreatitis** (inflammation of the pancreas), and Januvia's own US prescribing label warns about reports of pancreatitis in people taking it. Alcohol can also cause **delayed low blood sugar**, a risk that matters most if you take Januvia alongside insulin or a sulfonylurea such as glipizide. And if your pill is actually **Janumet**, which combines sitagliptin with metformin, the metformin half carries its own alcohol warning. This guide explains how the drug works, where alcohol fits in, and the warning signs that mean you should get help.

**The quick rules:** Ask your doctor or prescriber whether alcohol is OK for you specifically, and let them set the amount. If they say drinking is fine, never drink on an empty stomach, avoid binges, and check your blood sugar before bed if you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea. Know the signs of pancreatitis, especially severe upper stomach pain that may spread to your back, and get medical care right away if it happens. Check your label: if it says Janumet or sitagliptin/metformin, read the metformin section below too.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and the official prescribing information. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history, and you should not stop or change your Januvia dose on your own. **Talk to your doctor before drinking alcohol on Januvia**, especially if you have had pancreatitis or gallstones, take insulin or a sulfonylurea, take Janumet, have kidney or liver disease, have heart failure, or tend to have more than a couple of drinks at a time. **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US) if** you have severe stomach pain that won't go away (with or without vomiting or pain spreading to your back), a low blood sugar you can't bring up, confusion, or someone with diabetes who is very drowsy or won't wake up.

## What Januvia Does in Your Body

Januvia is the brand name for **sitagliptin**, a once-daily tablet for adults with type 2 diabetes. It belongs to a group of medicines called **DPP-4 inhibitors**, sometimes called "gliptins." Other drugs in the same group include saxagliptin (Onglyza), linagliptin (Tradjenta), and alogliptin (Nesina). Sitagliptin is also available combined with metformin as **Janumet** and Janumet XR, and generic versions of sitagliptin are now sold in the US.

To understand how it works, it helps to know about a pair of gut hormones called **incretins**. The main ones are GLP-1 and GIP. When you eat, your gut releases them, and they tell your pancreas to release insulin and tell the liver to make less sugar. They're part of the reason your body responds to a meal smoothly.

Incretins don't last long. An enzyme called **DPP-4** breaks them down within minutes. Januvia blocks that enzyme, so your own incretin hormones stick around longer and work harder. The result is more insulin after meals and less sugar coming out of the liver.

The key detail is that this effect is **glucose-dependent**. Incretins mainly boost insulin when your blood sugar is raised, and their effect fades as blood sugar returns to normal. That's the main reason Januvia, taken by itself or with metformin, has a low risk of causing hypoglycemia (low blood sugar). It's also why the alcohol story for Januvia is very different from the story for insulin or older pills like glipizide, which push insulin out regardless of what your blood sugar is doing.

### How Januvia is cleared

Most of each Januvia dose leaves your body unchanged in your urine. Only a small portion is processed by liver enzymes. That's useful to know for two reasons:

- **There's no meaningful liver-enzyme clash with alcohol.** Some drug-alcohol problems happen because both compete for, or alter, the same liver enzymes. That isn't the main issue here.
- **Your kidneys matter.** Because the kidneys do most of the clearing, the dose is lowered for people with reduced kidney function. Heavy drinking that leaves you badly dehydrated can strain the kidneys temporarily, and Januvia's label also mentions reports of worsening kidney function, sometimes needing dialysis. This is one more reason to avoid binge drinking and to rehydrate if you've been vomiting.

## Is It Safe to Drink Alcohol on Januvia?

For many people, an occasional, moderate drink is something their doctor is comfortable with. Januvia's prescribing information doesn't include a specific warning telling everyone to avoid alcohol, and there's no known direct interaction between sitagliptin and ethanol.

But "no direct interaction" isn't the same as "no risk." Your answer depends on a few things that only your prescriber can weigh:

- **Your pancreas history.** Have you ever had pancreatitis, gallstones, or very high triglycerides?
- **Your other diabetes medicines.** Januvia alone carries little hypoglycemia risk. Januvia plus insulin or a sulfonylurea carries real risk, and alcohol makes it worse.
- **Whether you take Janumet.** The metformin part has a label warning about excessive alcohol.
- **How you drink.** One glass of wine with dinner is a very different situation from five drinks on an empty stomach.
- **Your liver, kidneys, and heart.** All of these affect how your body handles both alcohol and diabetes.

General diabetes guidance, including from the American Diabetes Association, is that adults with diabetes who choose to drink should do so in moderation, with food, and with awareness of low blood sugar. Your own doctor's limit may be lower than any general guideline, and some people are best advised not to drink at all. That's a conversation to have, not a number to borrow from the internet.

## The Pancreatitis Question

This is the concern that makes Januvia's alcohol story worth a careful read.

### What the label says

Januvia's US prescribing information includes a warning about **acute pancreatitis**. After the drug went on the market, there were reports of pancreatitis in people taking it, including some severe cases (hemorrhagic or necrotizing pancreatitis) and some deaths. The label tells doctors to watch patients for signs of pancreatitis after starting Januvia and to stop the drug promptly if pancreatitis is suspected. It also notes that it isn't known whether people with a history of pancreatitis are at higher risk on Januvia.

It's important to keep this in proportion. These reports are rare, and the larger research picture on whether DPP-4 inhibitors actually cause pancreatitis is still debated. Large heart-safety trials of DPP-4 inhibitors, including one for sitagliptin, found pancreatitis was uncommon. Many experts consider the absolute risk small. But regulators considered it important enough to put on the label, and that's the part that matters when you add alcohol.

### Why alcohol matters here

Heavy alcohol use is one of the two leading causes of acute pancreatitis in adults, alongside gallstones. Long-term heavy drinking is also the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis. Alcohol can trigger inflammation in the pancreas, and in some people a single heavy binge can set off an attack.

So the concern isn't that sitagliptin and alcohol react with each other in a test tube. It's that you'd be combining a medicine with a labeled pancreatitis warning with one of the best-known pancreatitis triggers. There isn't strong evidence on whether the two together add up to a meaningfully higher risk than either alone. Until there is, the reasonable approach is caution, and especially avoiding binge drinking.

People with type 2 diabetes may also have other pancreatitis risk factors, such as gallstones or high triglycerides. Heavy drinking can raise triglycerides too. If any of these apply to you, it's worth asking your doctor directly whether alcohol is a good idea at all.

### Signs of pancreatitis to know

The classic sign is **severe pain in the upper abdomen** that:

- Comes on suddenly or builds over a few hours
- Often feels like it's boring through to your back
- Is persistent rather than coming and going
- May feel worse after eating or lying flat

It's often accompanied by **nausea and vomiting**, a tender belly, fever, or a fast heartbeat.

This is where alcohol makes things tricky. Nausea, vomiting, and an upset stomach are also common hangover symptoms, so it's easy to brush them off. The difference is the pain. A hangover stomach feels queasy and unsettled and improves over the day. Pancreatitis pain is severe, steady, centered high in the belly, and doesn't let up. If you're on Januvia and you have that kind of pain, get medical care right away, and tell the team you take sitagliptin. Don't take your next dose until a doctor has checked you.

## Low Blood Sugar: When It's a Real Risk

### Why Januvia alone rarely causes it

As explained above, Januvia's effect on insulin fades when your blood sugar drops toward normal. That built-in brake is why hypoglycemia is uncommon when Januvia is used alone or with metformin. Alcohol doesn't switch that brake off.

### How alcohol lowers blood sugar

Alcohol can cause low blood sugar in anyone with diabetes, through a different route. When you're not eating, your liver keeps your blood sugar up by releasing stored sugar and by making new glucose (a process called gluconeogenesis). Your liver also does most of the work of breaking down alcohol, and while it's busy with alcohol, it makes less new glucose.

Two features make this risky:

- **It's often delayed.** The drop can come hours after your last drink, overnight or the next morning, when you're asleep and can't notice it.
- **It looks like being drunk.** Confusion, slurred speech, unsteadiness, and drowsiness are signs of both low blood sugar and intoxication. You, your friends, or even medical staff might mistake one for the other.

If you want the fuller picture, our guide to [low blood sugar after drinking](/never-hungover/low-blood-sugar-after-drinking) explains the timing and what to do in more detail.

### The combinations that matter

The picture changes a lot depending on what else you take:

- **Januvia alone:** low risk of hypoglycemia, though alcohol can still lower blood sugar on its own, especially if you drink a lot without eating.
- **Januvia plus metformin (including Janumet):** still a fairly low hypoglycemia risk, but the metformin adds a separate alcohol concern (see below).
- **Januvia plus a sulfonylurea** (glipizide, glimepiride, glyburide): a real hypoglycemia risk. Januvia's label notes that a lower sulfonylurea dose may be needed to reduce the chance of lows. Alcohol on top raises that risk further. Our page on [glipizide and alcohol](/never-hungover/glipizide-and-alcohol) covers this in depth.
- **Januvia plus insulin:** the same story. The label notes a lower insulin dose may be needed, and alcohol can cause delayed lows.

If you take Januvia with insulin or a sulfonylurea, ask your doctor specifically how to handle drinking: whether to check your blood sugar before bed, what number should prompt a snack, and whether to adjust anything on days you drink. Don't make those adjustments on your own.

### Signs of low blood sugar

- Shakiness, sweating, or a pounding heart
- Sudden hunger
- Irritability, anxiety, or mood change
- Dizziness or blurred vision
- Confusion, trouble speaking, or poor coordination
- In severe cases, seizures or passing out

If you can, check your blood sugar. If it's low, follow the plan your care team gave you, usually fast-acting sugar such as glucose tablets or juice, then recheck. Carry glucose tablets and wear or carry diabetes ID when you drink, so others know what might be happening if you become confused.

## If You Take Janumet: The Metformin Part

A lot of people who search for Januvia actually take **Janumet**, the combination tablet with sitagliptin plus metformin. That matters, because metformin has its own alcohol warning.

Metformin's prescribing information, including Janumet's, carries a boxed warning about **lactic acidosis**, a rare but serious build-up of lactic acid in the blood. Excessive alcohol intake is listed as a risk factor, because alcohol makes it harder for the liver to clear lactate, and metformin also raises lactate levels slightly. The label advises patients to avoid excessive alcohol while taking it.

Lactic acidosis is rare, and it's mostly a concern with heavy drinking, binges, dehydration, or kidney problems. But the warning signs are worth knowing: unusual muscle pain, trouble breathing, unusual sleepiness, stomach pain with nausea or vomiting, feeling cold, dizziness, or a slow or irregular heartbeat. These need emergency care.

We cover this in depth in our guide to [metformin and alcohol](/never-hungover/metformin-and-alcohol). If you take Janumet, read that too, because the metformin part is the more direct alcohol concern of the two ingredients.

## Other Januvia Label Warnings Worth Knowing

These aren't alcohol warnings, but they're useful context if you're weighing how drinking fits with your health:

- **Heart failure.** Januvia's label includes a warning about heart failure, based on findings with other drugs in the DPP-4 class. If you have heart failure or kidney problems, your doctor will weigh this. Heavy drinking can also weaken the heart muscle over time, so this is another reason for caution if you have heart disease.
- **Kidney problems.** As mentioned above, the dose depends on kidney function, and the label mentions reports of worsening kidney function. Severe dehydration from heavy drinking or vomiting stresses the kidneys.
- **Serious allergic reactions.** Rarely, Januvia can cause swelling of the face, lips, or throat, severe rashes, or trouble breathing. These need emergency care.
- **Severe joint pain.** The label mentions reports of severe and disabling joint pain with DPP-4 inhibitors.
- **Bullous pemphigoid.** A rare skin condition causing large, fluid-filled blisters has been reported. Tell your doctor if you notice blisters.

None of these is common, but they're part of why your prescriber is the right person to decide what's safe for you.

## How Januvia Compares to Other Diabetes Medicines and Alcohol

It can help to see where Januvia sits among the medicines commonly used for type 2 diabetes. In plain terms:

- **Metformin:** low hypoglycemia risk alone; main alcohol concern is lactic acidosis with heavy drinking. See [metformin and alcohol](/never-hungover/metformin-and-alcohol).
- **Sulfonylureas such as glipizide:** the highest hypoglycemia risk among common pills, and alcohol can make lows worse and more delayed. See [glipizide and alcohol](/never-hungover/glipizide-and-alcohol).
- **SGLT2 inhibitors such as Jardiance:** main concern is ketoacidosis and dehydration with heavy drinking. See [Jardiance and alcohol](/never-hungover/jardiance-and-alcohol).
- **GLP-1 medicines such as Ozempic or Mounjaro:** these are related to Januvia in that they also work through incretin hormones, but they act much more strongly and are injected (or, for Rybelsus, taken by mouth). They also carry pancreatitis warnings and often cause nausea, which alcohol can make worse. See [Mounjaro and alcohol](/never-hungover/mounjaro-and-alcohol).
- **DPP-4 inhibitors such as Januvia:** low hypoglycemia risk alone; the alcohol concern is mainly about pancreatitis and about lows when combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea.

For a broader look at drinking with diabetes, including how to plan around meals and medicines, see our [guide to alcohol and blood sugar management](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025).

## If Your Doctor Says an Occasional Drink Is OK

If you and your prescriber agree that some alcohol is fine, these habits lower the risks discussed above:

- **Let your prescriber set the limit.** Stick to the amount they gave you, not what friends are having.
- **Eat first and while drinking.** Food slows alcohol absorption and helps protect against low blood sugar. Don't use alcohol as a meal replacement.
- **Avoid binges.** Several drinks in a short time is the pattern most linked to pancreatitis attacks, dangerous lows, and dehydration.
- **Pace with water.** Alternating alcoholic drinks with water helps with hydration and slows how much you drink.
- **Watch sugary mixers and sweet drinks.** They can push your sugar up first, and the alcohol can bring it down later, which makes it harder to read what's happening.
- **Check your blood sugar** before drinking, before bed, and in the morning, if you use a meter and take insulin or a sulfonylurea. A bedtime snack may be part of your doctor's plan.
- **Don't drink alone if you're prone to lows**, and make sure someone with you knows you have diabetes and how to help.
- **Keep taking Januvia as prescribed.** Don't skip or double doses because you plan to drink unless your prescriber has told you to. Skipping doses doesn't make alcohol safer, and changing your routine can upset your blood sugar control.

### Who should be especially careful, or not drink

Ask your doctor directly before drinking if any of these apply. For some of these, the advice may be not to drink at all:

- You've had pancreatitis, even once
- You have gallstones or very high triglycerides
- You take insulin or a sulfonylurea and have had lows before
- You take Janumet and have kidney problems
- You have liver disease, including fatty liver
- You have heart failure
- You're pregnant or trying to become pregnant
- You find it hard to stick to a limit once you start drinking

If cutting back has been hard for you, that's worth mentioning to your doctor too. They can help, and it's useful information for managing your diabetes.

## The Morning After on Januvia

A hangover on Januvia mostly looks like a hangover on anything else: headache, tiredness, thirst, and an unsettled stomach. A few things are different, though.

- **Eat breakfast.** Skipping food the morning after raises the risk of a delayed low, especially if you take insulin or a sulfonylurea.
- **Rehydrate.** Water, plus an electrolyte drink if you've been sweating or vomiting. Pick a low-sugar option if you're watching your glucose. Our page on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) explains why the thirst happens.
- **Check your blood sugar** if you have a meter and take medicines that can cause lows.
- **Pay attention to stomach pain.** Queasiness that fades as the day goes on is typical. Severe, steady upper belly pain, especially spreading to your back, is not a hangover symptom to wait out on Januvia. Get it checked.
- **Be careful with painkillers.** Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs can irritate the stomach and, especially when you're dehydrated, the kidneys. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is harder on the liver after drinking. Use the lowest label dose, with food, and ask a pharmacist if you're unsure what fits with your medicines.

## When to See a Doctor

**Call your doctor or care team soon if:**

- You've had stomach pain or nausea that comes back after drinking
- You've been vomiting, or can't eat or drink normally, for more than a few hours
- You've had low blood sugar episodes after drinking
- You regularly have more than a couple of drinks at a time and you're on Januvia or Janumet
- You notice new swelling in your legs, shortness of breath, or rapid weight gain
- You develop blisters, a new rash, or severe joint pain

**Get emergency care right away (call 911 in the US) if you have:**

- Severe abdominal pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting or pain spreading to your back
- A low blood sugar you can't bring up, or someone with diabetes who is confused, very drowsy, or won't wake up
- Fast or labored breathing, unusual muscle pain, or unusual sleepiness, especially if you take Janumet
- Swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or trouble breathing or swallowing

Tell the medical team that you take sitagliptin (Januvia or Janumet), any other diabetes medicines, and how much you've had to drink. That information helps them check for pancreatitis, low blood sugar, and lactic acidosis quickly.

## Can a Supplement Help?

Some people who drink occasionally look at supplements to make the morning after easier. Here's an honest view, with the caveat that this matters much less than the basics above.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. There is no good evidence that DHM lowers the risk of pancreatitis, low blood sugar, or lactic acidosis, and it doesn't make heavy drinking safe on Januvia or Janumet. It also hasn't been studied in people taking DPP-4 inhibitors. Some lab and animal research suggests DHM may affect glucose handling, which is one more reason to check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding it, as you would with any supplement when you have diabetes.

If you and your doctor decide it's reasonable for an occasional night out, a well-reviewed option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), and the premium [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) adds other ingredients. Read the full label, because some hangover products contain added sugar or other ingredients you'll want your pharmacist to review. Our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known and unknown about combining DHM with prescription drugs.

## Key Takeaways

- Januvia (sitagliptin) has no known direct chemical interaction with alcohol, and on its own it rarely causes low blood sugar.
- The main concern is pancreatitis. Januvia's label warns about it, and heavy drinking is a leading cause of it. Avoid binges and know the warning signs.
- Alcohol can cause delayed low blood sugar, which matters most if you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea.
- If you take Janumet, the metformin part carries a label warning about lactic acidosis with excessive alcohol.
- Your prescriber should decide whether you can drink and how much. Don't change your Januvia dose on your own.

Some people move from Januvia to an injectable medicine in the same broad family (both work through the incretin system). If that's you, see our guides on [Victoza and alcohol](/never-hungover/victoza-and-alcohol), [Wegovy and alcohol](/never-hungover/wegovy-and-alcohol), and [Trulicity and alcohol](/never-hungover/trulicity-and-alcohol).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Januvia?**

Many people can have an occasional drink on Januvia if their doctor agrees. There's no known direct chemical interaction between sitagliptin and alcohol. The concerns are indirect: heavy drinking is a leading cause of pancreatitis, which is a labeled warning for Januvia, and alcohol can cause delayed low blood sugar, especially if you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea. Ask your prescriber what's safe for you.

**Does Januvia cause low blood sugar with alcohol?**

Januvia alone rarely causes low blood sugar because its effect on insulin fades as blood sugar falls. Alcohol, though, can lower blood sugar on its own by slowing the liver's glucose production, often hours later. The risk is much higher if you take Januvia with insulin or a sulfonylurea like glipizide. Eat when you drink and check your blood sugar if your doctor has asked you to.

**Can alcohol and Januvia cause pancreatitis?**

Januvia's label warns about reports of pancreatitis in people taking it, and heavy alcohol use is one of the most common causes of pancreatitis in general. It isn't clearly established whether the two together raise the risk more than either alone, but combining them calls for caution, especially avoiding binge drinking. Severe upper stomach pain that won't go away, sometimes spreading to the back, needs urgent medical care.

**Is it safe to drink on Janumet?**

Janumet contains sitagliptin plus metformin, and the metformin part carries a boxed warning about lactic acidosis, with excessive alcohol listed as a risk factor. The label advises avoiding excessive alcohol. An occasional drink may be acceptable if your doctor says so, but heavy drinking or binges on Janumet are a real concern. Talk to your prescriber before drinking.

**Should I skip my Januvia dose if I'm going to drink?**

Not unless your prescriber tells you to. Skipping a dose doesn't make alcohol safer and can upset your blood sugar control. Take Januvia as prescribed, and focus on drinking only what your doctor has said is OK, with food. If you take insulin or a sulfonylurea too, ask your doctor whether anything should change on days you drink.

**How long after taking Januvia can I drink alcohol?**

There's no official waiting period, because Januvia is taken once daily and works steadily over the day rather than peaking in a way alcohol clashes with. Timing matters less than how much you drink and whether you eat. If your doctor says alcohol is fine, have it with a meal and avoid large amounts.

**What are the warning signs I should watch for after drinking on Januvia?**

Watch for severe, steady upper stomach pain, possibly spreading to your back, with or without nausea and vomiting, which can signal pancreatitis. Also watch for signs of low blood sugar such as shakiness, sweating, confusion, or drowsiness, and, if you take Janumet, unusual muscle pain, trouble breathing, or unusual sleepiness. Any of these after drinking needs prompt medical attention.

**Can I take DHM with Januvia?**

DHM hasn't been studied in people taking Januvia or other DPP-4 inhibitors, and there's no good evidence it reduces the risks of drinking on this medicine. Some lab and animal research suggests DHM may affect glucose handling, so ask your doctor or pharmacist before combining it with any diabetes medicine.
